summary: Surveys peer-to-peer systems, giving a definition and several ways to classify them. It describes which kinds of applications can be built with P2P technology and gives examples of P2P applications in use. It is informational.

eli5.summary: In a peer-to-peer system, everyone shares and helps instead of relying on one big server. This document explains the different kinds of such systems and what they are good for.

questions: what are the types of p2p systems
when should i use peer-to-peer instead of client-server
subtitle: What counts as peer-to-peer, how P2P systems are classified, and when the architecture is a good choice.

tldr.problem: Engineers lack a common understanding of P2P systems, and many in the industry equate P2P with illegal activity.
tldr.mechanism: The IAB survey defines a P2P system as one whose elements share resources and both provide and request services, then classifies P2P systems (mainly by how data is indexed), reviews application domains, and weighs trade-offs against client-server designs.
tldr.outcome: It gives guidance rather than rules: whether P2P fits depends on the application, its context and cost.

facts.label: Application domains
facts.value: Content distribution, distributed computing, collaboration, platforms

facts.label: P2P test
facts.value: Peers both provide and request services

today: RFC 5694 is an Informational IAB document and, per the unit metadata, has not been obsoleted or updated.

sections.title: Why a P2P Survey
sections.content:
RFC 5694 is a survey published on behalf of the IAB. It starts from two observations: engineers designing systems do not share a common understanding of P2P, and many in the telecom and datacom industries believe P2P is synonymous with illegal activity such as illegal content exchange or P2P botnets.

The goal is to discuss the trade-offs in deciding whether an application is best built as P2P or in another model such as client-server, and to give architectural guidelines for that decision. The RFC stresses with examples that P2P can implement legitimate applications and business models.
sections.eli5: Some people think sharing networks are only for sneaky things. This document says no, and helps you pick the right tool.

sections.title: Defining a P2P System
sections.content:
The RFC calls a system P2P if the elements that form it share their resources to provide the service the system was designed for, and the elements both provide services to and request services from other elements. In practice a few exceptions are allowed: a system with a centralized enrollment server can still be P2P, but one where most endpoints are only clients could not strictly be called P2P.

It then applies the test to four systems:

  • DNS is not P2P, because resolvers request services but do not provide them.
  • Traditional SIP is not P2P, because user agents are only involved in transactions that benefit themselves.
  • P2PSIP is P2P, because nodes store contact information for other user agents in an overlay and help with rendezvous that does not benefit themselves directly.
  • BitTorrent is P2P, because endpoints in a swarm both download and upload pieces. A swarm made mostly of always-seeding infrastructure nodes would not strictly qualify.
sections.eli5: It is a sharing club only if every member both borrows and lends. A library where you only borrow is not that kind of club.

sections.title: Functions and Taxonomies
sections.content:
The RFC separates functions independent of the service (enrollment and peer discovery, sometimes done centrally by a bootstrap server) from service-dependent ones: data indexing, data storage, computation and message transport.

It calls the way data is indexed the most useful basis for classification. An index can be centralized, local or distributed; the RFC names Napster, early Gnutella (up to version 0.4) and DHT-based systems as examples of each. Indexes can also be semantic or semantic-free. Other taxonomies split systems into hybrid versus pure, and unstructured versus structured, though the border between the last two has blurred.

The RFC argues that talking about first, second and third generations of P2P is not useful technically, because authors define the generations differently and the labels suggest later is better.
sections.eli5: The most useful question is: who keeps the list of who has what? One big list, each person's own list, or a list split among many people.

sections.title: Application Domains
sections.content:
P2P applications fall into four domains: content distribution, distributed computing, collaboration and platforms.

Content distribution is the best known. Its main advantage is scalability: the peer with the original content does not have to send everything to everyone. The RFC lists legitimate uses such as pre-recorded TV, Linux distributions, game updates and live TV by authorized parties. Users, CDN operators and network operators each prefer different peer selection.

Distributed computing splits a task into independent subtasks. The RFC says Grid computing, SETI@home, MapReduce and P2P botnets cannot strictly be called P2P because requests come from a central node.

Collaboration covers VoIP and instant messaging, such as P2PSIP. Platforms, such as JXTA, provide peer discovery, grouping and communication for applications built on top.
sections.eli5: People share files, lend computer time, chat, or build tools that others build on. Just because some people share things they should not does not make the sharing itself wrong.

sections.title: Trade-Offs and Guidance
sections.content:
The RFC says there is no definitive rule for choosing P2P, and operational requirements must be analyzed case by case. It does give pointers.

  • No infrastructure: ad hoc systems and disaster areas are good candidates.
  • Scalability: peers add capacity as they join, but running a DHT requires nontrivial operational effort.
  • Robustness: peers are not expected to be highly available, so P2P systems use data replication and redundant routing table entries.
  • Performance: depends on the task; a well-dimensioned central database may be faster than a DHT.
  • Incentives: free riders hurt performance.
  • Energy: a client-server system generally uses less overall, but battery-powered peers face extra challenges.

Cost is often the most important factor: if upgrading a server is cheap, client-server may be best; if a highly available server is expensive, P2P may win.
sections.eli5: Sharing is great when there is no shop nearby or too many people for one shop. If the shop is cheap and open all day, just use the shop.

sections.title: Security of P2P Systems
sections.content:
If all nodes are fully trusted, a P2P architecture can reach a high level of security. If nodes may be malicious, security is harder than in non-P2P systems because ownership is distributed and there is no central control. P2P systems have fewer central elements to attack, but peers can harvest IP addresses passively, and intermediate peers can mount on-path attacks.

The RFC names threats and mitigations: the Sybil attack (control how peers get identifiers), eavesdropping (encrypt parts not needed for routing), forgery (peer and message authentication), storage abuse (quotas, data object authentication, lifetimes), refusal to store (replication and parallel searches), the Eclipse attack (structural constraints or node degree bounds) and churn attacks (limit churn per node).
sections.eli5: When strangers help carry your mail, some could peek, lie or pretend to be someone else. The defenses are locks, name checks and asking several helpers.
